section_summary: This section documents federal and public concern over Japanese espionage, propaganda, naval observation, and influence in the United States during 1937–1938. It includes the Farnsworth espionage prosecution, proposed transfer of radio technology to Japan, citizen reports about Japanese residents and travelers, investigations of propaganda distribution, alleged surveillance by fishing vessels, and monitoring of Japanese shortwave broadcasts. State, Navy, Justice, congressional, and White House correspondence shows officials assessing these claims while frequently treating public allegations cautiously.

subfiles.title: Subpoena in United States v. John S. Farnsworth
subfiles.from: Supreme Court of the District of Columbia
subfiles.to: Department of State, Attention: Chief Clerk
subfiles.about: The subpoena demands testimony and records concerning Japanese government representatives and naval attachés in Washington between 1933 and 1936.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State is commanded to appear for the United States in the criminal prosecution of John S. Farnsworth. Requested records include the names and Washington addresses of accredited Japanese Imperial Government representatives, the offices of Japanese naval attachés, and the dates on which those persons arrived and departed. The appearance date is February 2, 1937.

subfiles.title: Pacent Engineering request and Rochelle-salt questionnaires
subfiles.from: Louis Gerard Pacent, Pacent Engineering Corporation
subfiles.about: Pacent requests permission to answer paid technical questionnaires from Matsushita Radio Manufacturing Company in Japan.
subfiles.summary: Pacent Engineering says Matsushita has asked it to provide technical commercial information in exchange for a fee and offers to submit future questionnaires to the State Department before answering. The enclosed material asks about the crystallization, bonding, moisture protection, strengthening, and tin electrodes of Rochelle-salt components. A second enclosure describes Matsushita's laboratory experiments and difficulties producing clear, durable crystals.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Pacent Engineering
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department advises that Pacent may answer Matsushita's questionnaires provided it does not disclose military secrets.
subfiles.summary: The reply states that no treaty or statute bars the proposed technical service so long as the answers reveal no information affecting national defense. Pacent is directed to the Espionage Act of June 15, 1917, and invited to submit doubtful material for consultation with appropriate authorities. The Department also accepts Pacent's offer to forward later questionnaires confidentially.

subfiles.title: Notification to the Secretary of the Navy concerning Pacent Engineering
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards the Pacent correspondence concerning technical information for Matsushita Radio Manufacturing Company.
subfiles.summary: The Navy receives copies of Pacent's March 19 letter and the Department's reply. The note identifies the proposed recipient as Matsushita Radio Manufacturing Company of Osaka and describes the material as technical commercial information.

subfiles.title: Notification to the Secretary of War concerning Pacent Engineering
subfiles.about: The State Department forwards the Pacent correspondence about supplying technical information to Matsushita.
subfiles.summary: The War Department is sent copies of Pacent's letter and the State Department's response. The notification records the proposed provision of commercial technical information to the Osaka radio manufacturer.

subfiles.title: Alyce Jones letter alleging Japanese religious propaganda and spying
subfiles.about: Jones uses newspaper clippings to allege that Buddhist activity and Japanese imagery in the United States conceal propaganda and espionage.
subfiles.summary: Jones describes five clippings as evidence of Japanese territorial methods, Buddhist propaganda, questionable Christian conversions, and other allegedly deceptive practices. She claims pictures and Buddhist advertising may transmit secret messages among Japanese Americans. She urges surveillance, fingerprinting, restrictions on land ownership, removal of Japanese displays, and abolition of Buddhist temples.

subfiles.title: D. M. Robertson letter concerning Japanese activity in Chatham
subfiles.about: Robertson reports Japanese men in Chatham and expresses concern about Japanese-made goods and social activity.
subfiles.summary: The surviving fragment says five Japanese men were in Chatham with white women, taking pictures and visiting stores. Robertson also complains that purchasers discover goods marked “made in Japan.” The opening and much contextual detail are missing or illegible.

subfiles.title: Barbara Kessner report of Japanese passengers traveling to Galveston
subfiles.about: A train hostess confidentially reports recurring Japanese passengers traveling toward the Galveston seaport.
subfiles.summary: Kessner says that while working on Burlington–Rock Island trains between Houston and Fort Worth she repeatedly observed well-educated Japanese men bound for Galveston. Although she found them desirable passengers, she wondered whether wartime tensions made their repeated travel to the port suspicious. She asks that the report remain confidential and closes with praise for Roosevelt's popularity in the South.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment to Barbara Kessner
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges Kessner's White House-referred report about passengers making frequent trips to Galveston.
subfiles.summary: Hamilton states that Kessner's letter has received careful attention. He thanks her for bringing the matter to the government's notice without commenting on the substance of her suspicions.

subfiles.title: Virginia E. Jenckes inquiry about the Farnsworth espionage case
subfiles.about: Jenckes requests the facts of the Farnsworth case and asks whether Japan made representations or expressed regret.
subfiles.summary: Jenckes notes that Lieutenant Commander Farnsworth was convicted and sent to the federal prison at Atlanta for selling confidential Navy information to Japan. She requests an account for her use as a member of Congress. Her specific question concerns any Japanese governmental apology, protest, or expression of regret.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull reply to Virginia E. Jenckes
subfiles.about: Hull directs Jenckes to the Justice Department for case details and states that Japan made no representations or apologies.
subfiles.summary: Hull explains that the Farnsworth prosecution fell under the jurisdiction of the Department of Justice. He recommends that Jenckes seek the factual record there. He directly answers that the Japanese Government neither made representations nor expressed regret.

subfiles.title: Report of Japanese propaganda funds allocated in the United States
subfiles.about: An internal note records a report that Japan allocated $175,000 for propaganda in the United States, including $100,000 for Ambassador Saitō.
subfiles.summary: Colonel Strong is identified as the source of information considered reliable. According to the report, the Japanese Government distributed the funds to its American representatives during the preceding six weeks. The largest stated allocation went to Ambassador Saitō.

subfiles.title: File charge-out record
subfiles.about: The form records later charges and transfers of items from the archival file.
subfiles.summary: This is a later administrative charge-out sheet rather than substantive 1930s correspondence. It contains several handwritten names and dates indicating custody of file items from 1957 into the 1970s.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference to file 861.01h.11/62
subfiles.about: The sheet directs researchers to another file for a related government document.
subfiles.summary: The mostly blank form refers the reader to file 861.01h.11/62. Its subject notation is fragmentary, and no substantive description survives beyond the cross-reference and date.

subfiles.title: Special-agent report concerning Toichiro Tsuge
subfiles.from: J. F. Fit, Special Agent in Charge
subfiles.to: R. C. Bannerman, Chief Special Agent
subfiles.about: A special agent reports Mabel Stevens's suspicions concerning Japanese tenant Toichiro Tsuge and his relatives.
subfiles.summary: Stevens had rented houses in Mamaroneck to Tsuge and to relatives Takeo and Mrs. Suyemasa, and reported that Tsuge was leaving for Japan after working for Mitsui in New York. She became alarmed when Mrs. Suyemasa defended Japan's conduct in China and predicted war with the United States within two years. The reporting agent regarded the information as unimportant, though later routing notes indicate consultation with naval intelligence.

subfiles.title: Confidential referral of the Tsuge report to the Navy
subfiles.about: The State Department confidentially forwards the report of Mabel Stevens's statements about Toichiro Tsuge.
subfiles.summary: The note transmits a memorandum drawn from information received by the Department. It asks no specific action but supplies the Navy with the allegations for its confidential information.

subfiles.title: Peggy Jean Simmons letter alleging Japanese information gathering
subfiles.about: A Los Angeles schoolgirl reports statements allegedly made by Japanese classmates about sending information to Japan and a parent serving as a special agent.
subfiles.summary: Simmons says she attended Berendo Junior High School with many Japanese children. She claims one girl disclosed that Japanese people in Los Angeles and elsewhere in California sent information to Japan, while another said her father traveled from Japan to American coastal cities as a special Japanese agent. Simmons presents the information as an effort to help her country.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Peggy Jean Simmons's letter
subfiles.about: The Department acknowledges the White House referral and says appropriate attention has been given to Simmons's report.
subfiles.summary: The brief form letter identifies Simmons's communication by its November 25 date. It provides no assessment of the allegations and merely confirms official attention.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference concerning alleged efforts to influence American newspapers
subfiles.about: The sheet points to a report from the assistant naval attaché at Shanghai about buying off American newspapers and reporters to preserve neutrality.
subfiles.summary: The original item is filed in a Navy Department confidential series rather than reproduced here. Its indexed subject is an allegation that money was being used to influence American press coverage and sustain United States neutrality.

subfiles.title: Assessment of propaganda enclosures from the Japanese Consulate in Chicago
subfiles.about: The memorandum inventories Japanese-viewpoint publications and considers whether a foreign consul should distribute privately published propaganda.
subfiles.summary: The enclosures came from publishers in New York, San Francisco, Tokyo, Chicago, and Osaka and generally presented Japan's position in the Sino-Japanese conflict. A handbill from the Society for Promotion of Pacific Peace is characterized as especially blatant and includes a Boake Carter column attacking named State Department officials and British influence. The memorandum identifies both the general propriety of consular propaganda distribution and the narrower problem of circulating criticism of the United States government.

subfiles.title: Allan S. Farquhar letter transmitting Japanese propaganda
subfiles.from: Allan S. Farquhar, Acting Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Farquhar forwards propaganda obtained from the Japanese consulate in Chicago and questions the consul's distribution of a handbill.
subfiles.summary: Farquhar reports that the Chicago consulate was filled with boxes of propaganda then being distributed by the consul. He calls particular attention to the handbill “Let's Suppose...” and says the propriety of its consular distribution has been questioned.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment to Farquhar
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Farquhar's propaganda exhibits and states that the issue is under consideration.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck confirms receipt of printed material concerning the Far Eastern conflict from the Japanese consulate in Chicago. He thanks Farquhar for drawing attention to the disputed consular distribution.

subfiles.title: “Chinese War to Aid U.S., Says Tokyo Consul Here”
subfiles.about: The clipping reports Japanese consul general Hideo Mizutani's defense of Japan's war in China before a Chicago military club.
subfiles.summary: Mizutani blames foreign encouragement and Soviet assistance for prolonging China's resistance and predicts a division between communist and Japanese-friendly regions. He claims Japan's actions will benefit American trade, citing rising United States exports to Manchukuo. He portrays Japan as fighting communism and advancing America's interest in stable government and purchasing power.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Arthur B. Kepler concerning investigative work
subfiles.about: Private investigator Arthur Kepler offers to gain Japanese confidence and enter Japanese employment for investigative purposes.
subfiles.summary: Kepler says he works independently, has Japanese contacts, and could infiltrate their employment if the Department needed an investigation. He recounts an earlier approach from a Japanese acquaintance named Kasuda and recent advice from two postmen to contact the Japanese Embassy. Ballantine declines the offer while saying he will remember it should a suitable matter arise.

subfiles.title: Conversation with Alexander Resin about foreign propaganda
subfiles.about: Research fellow Alexander Resin asks the Department for leads on the entry, distribution, authorship, and printing of foreign propaganda.
subfiles.summary: Resin is studying foreign propaganda under a New York University fellowship and seeks information about its movement through the United States. He specifically asks about the authorship and printing of “Sino-Japanese Crisis of 1937,” distributed by the Japanese Chamber of Commerce of New York. Ballantine promises to investigate and suggests a later meeting.

subfiles.title: Citizen letter proposing measures to prevent war
subfiles.about: A heavily degraded letter proposes economic, military, and legal measures intended to reduce war and foreign entanglements.
subfiles.summary: The writer discusses military preparedness, peace bonds, national ownership of munitions factories, conscription, war profiteering, and the World Court. The letter argues that private munitions profits and foreign investments contribute to conflict and suggests stronger national economic controls. Much of the wording, including the sender's identity, is obscured by poor OCR.

subfiles.title: Magazine excerpt on American trade, shipping, and alleged Japanese “spy” fishing boats
subfiles.from: Boake Carter, Guenther Reinhardt, and other magazine contributors
subfiles.about: The excerpt combines arguments for hemispheric trade and merchant shipping with allegations that Japanese-owned fishing boats could serve as spy, mine-laying, or torpedo craft.
subfiles.summary: Boake Carter's “Is Uncle Sam Blind?” argues that the United States should concentrate on commerce with Latin America, rebuild its merchant marine, and avoid entanglement in European and Asian conflicts. Guenther Reinhardt's article claims Japanese-controlled tuna boats observed naval exercises, photographed defenses, and could rapidly be converted into mine layers or torpedo boats. The packet also contains intervening magazine material on physical fitness, Roosevelt, advertising, and quiz answers.

subfiles.title: Alfred E. Chriske letter urging a survey of Japanese activity
subfiles.about: Chriske urges a comprehensive federal survey of Japanese immigration, fishing vessels, intelligence networks, and propaganda on the West Coast.
subfiles.summary: Chriske alleges that Japanese fishermen use radio-equipped vessels and floating canneries to communicate with liners and smuggle aliens or contraband ashore. He portrays Japanese residents, including American citizens, as a disciplined intelligence network serving Emperor Hirohito. He recommends fingerprinting, reciprocal residence restrictions, and a counterpropaganda bureau under presidential supervision, while offering his own cooperation.

subfiles.title: Otto E. Naegele letter and clipping about Japanese naval officers
subfiles.about: Naegele cites the detention of two Japanese naval officers near a Boston bridge as evidence that Japanese photographers seek militarily significant sites.
subfiles.summary: Naegele argues that the officers should be treated as spies and returned to Japan rather than accepted as harmless tourists. The enclosed Associated Press clipping reports that Lieutenant Commander Nishimura and Engineering Officer S. Ito were questioned after photographing near a bridge over the Charles River. Police released them after accepting their explanation that they were photography enthusiasts with valid passports.

subfiles.title: State Department acknowledgment to Otto E. Naegele
subfiles.from: Maxwell M. Hamilton, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Hamilton acknowledges Naegele's letter and clipping about the questioning of two Japanese officers in Boston.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that Naegele's views and the newspaper report have received careful consideration. Hamilton thanks him for the spirit that prompted the communication without endorsing its conclusions.

subfiles.title: Justice Department referral of Earl Nicholas's radio report
subfiles.from: Brien McMahon, for the Attorney General
subfiles.about: The Justice Department forwards Earl Nicholas's allegations about Japanese radio promotion of an investment corporation connected with occupied China.
subfiles.summary: McMahon requests appropriate attention and a reply to Nicholas. The referral describes the reported concern as the “Encorporate Re-habitation & Trade Development Corporation,” allegedly associated with Japan's invasion and conquest of China. Justice had not separately acknowledged the citizen's letter.

subfiles.title: Earl Nicholas letter and typed transcription concerning Tokyo shortwave broadcasts
subfiles.about: Nicholas reports monitoring Tokyo station JZJ and alleges that Japanese broadcasts solicit American investment in a corporation supporting occupation in North China.
subfiles.summary: Nicholas says his radios near Salina receive multilingual broadcasts from Tokyo directed toward the Malay Straits, Philippines, Indochina, and Australia. He alleges that Japan is promoting stock in a rehabilitation and trade-development corporation in occupied North China, using foreign investment to finance the war and replace Chinese currency with Japanese money. He asks whether neutrality law can restrain Americans who finance or supply either side, offers to let government observers transcribe the broadcasts, and also reports hearing Tokyo's acknowledgment of the American Panay damage claim. Pages 357–369 contain the difficult handwritten original, while pages 370–374 provide a typed transcription.

subfiles.title: Naval Intelligence report on Suma's West Coast tour
subfiles.from: Ralston S. Holmes, Director of Naval Intelligence
subfiles.about: Holmes reports Japanese diplomat Suma's meetings with American-born Japanese citizens and his optimistic statements about Japan's position in China.
subfiles.summary: Suma had visited Los Angeles and San Francisco and was expected to continue to Portland and Seattle while surveying conditions among Japanese communities. He reportedly said the European situation would give Japan a free hand in China, that American attitudes improved after the fall of Nanjing, and that the anti-Japanese boycott was driven by communist propaganda. Holmes encloses a related press clipping.

subfiles.title: Hornbeck acknowledgment of the Suma report
subfiles.about: Hornbeck acknowledges Holmes's letter and returns the press clippings about Suma's Pacific Coast activities.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck says he read the report and enclosures with interest. He thanks Holmes for bringing Suma's travel and public statements to the Department's attention and returns the clippings.

subfiles.title: Memorandum reviewing Japanese propaganda distributed through the Chicago consulate
subfiles.about: The memorandum inventories Japanese and American publications distributed through the Chicago consulate and evaluates their propagandistic character.
subfiles.summary: The listed publications include pictorial primers, the Tokyo Gazette, pamphlets on the Sino-Japanese conflict, the Osaka Mainichi, and American-produced materials from New York, California, and Chicago. The memorandum distinguishes useful or ordinary publications from material described as deliberately misleading propaganda for English-speaking audiences. Its discussion continues beyond page 378 and therefore remains incomplete in this section.
